query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 with an fcc matrix, selective oxidation of reactive elements (Al and Ti) under elevated-temperature oxidizing conditions leads to the formation of non-protective, discontinuous oxide scales at grain boundaries. This oxide-induced embrittlement promotes micro-cracking and eventual catastrophic failure, while in reducing environments, insufficient protective scale formation may allow dealloying and internal stress buildup that similarly predispose the alloy to failure.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized, as-built fcc matrix alloy with minimal pre-existing oxidation or segregation arising from additive manufacturing.
generation.intervention: Systematic alteration of the gas environment, where samples are exposed to controlled oxidizing versus reducing atmospheres at elevated temperatures.
generation.conditions: Exposure at temperatures between approximately 600°C and 1000°C for defined time periods; atmospheres with well-controlled oxygen partial pressures to simulate oxidizing and reducing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries where reactive element oxidation occurs, leading to local embrittlement and microstructural degradation.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, reactive elements (Al and Ti) preferentially oxidize to form non-uniform and non-protective oxide scales that initiate grain boundary embrittlement and micro-cracking. In contrast, reducing conditions can inhibit the formation of a continuous protective oxide, potentially resulting in compositional instability and stress accumulation, both of which contribute to catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline, samples exposed to oxidizing environments will exhibit increased grain boundary oxide scale formation, more pronounced micro-cracking, and reduced ductility leading to catastrophic failure at high exposures. Samples in reducing conditions may show less surface oxidation but increased signs of internal stress and dealloying, also predisposing the material to failure after prolonged exposure.
generation.baseline: As-manufactured alloy with minimal oxide scale formation, intact grain boundary integrity, and satisfactory mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies for high-temperature exposures (600°C–1000°C) under controlled gas atmospheres where oxygen partial pressures distinctly label oxidizing versus reducing environments.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature thresholds for transition between protective and non-protective oxide behavior and the kinetics of oxidation versus dealloying mechanisms remain to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple sets of identical as-manufactured alloy samples. Expose each set to either an oxidizing or reducing atmosphere at set temperatures (e.g., 700°C, 800°C, 900°C) for predetermined durations. Use consistent sample geometries and controlled exposure times to ensure comparability.
measurements: High-resolution scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to evaluate oxide scale morphology and grain boundary integrity.
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping to assess elemental distribution and extent of oxidation at grain boundaries.
Mechanical testing (e.g., tensile, fracture toughness tests) to quantify changes in ductility and identify catastrophic failure events.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under oxidizing conditions, the samples do not exhibit a significantly higher incidence of grain boundary oxide formation, micro-cracking, and reduced mechanical performance relative to the baseline, or if reducing conditions do not show evidence of internal stress buildup or dealloying leading to failure, then the hypothesis is falsified.

recalled_precedents.finding: Their work showed that selective oxidation of reactive elements like Al and Ti can lead to non-protective scale formation and subsequent grain boundary embrittlement, correlating increased reactive element activity with accelerated degradation.
